title: Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto (Finland) - TSV/40/2018
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
In April 2018, the DPA received a complaint stating that the city of Espoo (the controller) was using Google's digital learning tools in a school without obtaining consent from pupils’ (the data subjects’) parents.
The controller clarified that it used a number of Google applications for educational purposes, including Google Classroom, Google Drive, and Google Docs. It invoked Article 6(1)(c) GDPR as the legal basis for the processing. According to the controller, the processing of personal data in connection with using these services was necessary to comply with the obligation to provide basic education laid down in the Finnish Basic Education Act.
The DPA issued a decision in case 1509/452/18 in December 2021. This decision was appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, which referred the case back to the DPA in its decision KHO:2025:29 in April 2025. The Supreme Administrative Court held that the DPA could not conclude Article 6(1)(c) GDPR was not applicable in any respect as a legal basis for the processing.
In the present proceedings, the DPA was to decide the extent to which the controller could invoke the compliance with a legal obligation as a legal basis for the processing of personal data related to the use of Google’s digital learning tools.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA ordered the controller to ensure that the personal data of pupils collected in connection with the use of Google's digital learning tools was solely processed for the purpose of fulfilling the controller's educational obligations. The processing could be based on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR only under these conditions. 
The DPA held that the controller could invoke Article 6(1)(c) GDPR as a legal basis for the use of learning tools essential to teaching. In addition, the processing must be carried out solely to fulfill educational obligations. The DPA pointed out that this legal basis applies to the use of tools that are central to teaching, such as text editors, calendars, email, presentation software, and programs intended for subject-specific instruction (such as language or math applications).
When assessing the necessity requirement, the DPA took into account that digital learning tools can enable the extensive and long-term collection and other processing of school-aged children’s personal data by and for the benefit of external entities. Therefore, it held that the controller may not disclose or otherwise grant access to this data to the controller or other parties in a way that allows the controller to process the data for its own purposes, such as developing the learning tools or other services.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 615/2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject, an employee of a municipal agency, sent a certified email to the Municipality of Aprilia (the controller), requesting a meeting with its Extraordinary Commission to report alleged mismanagement and workplace bullying.
Instead of arranging the meeting or seeking further information, the controller forwarded the email, including the data subject's identity and email address, to his employer. The controller requested a report on the employee and the allegations raised. Following the disclosure, the employer initiated disciplinary proceedings against the data subject, resulting in his dismissal. The controller subsequently decided not to arrange the requested meeting.
The data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA. The controller argued that the disclosure was necessary to assess the credibility of the allegations and exercise its supervisory powers under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR. It also maintained that the employer's subsequent disciplinary decisions were independent of its disclosure.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that the controller had unlawfully disclosed the data subject's personal data without an appropriate legal basis, in violation of Articles 5(1)(a), (b) and (c) and 6(1)(c) and (e), (2) and (3)(b) GDPR.
First, the DPA held that the controller's general administrative and supervisory powers did not provide an adequate legal basis for disclosing the data subject's complaint and identity to his employer. The provisions invoked by the controller did not authorise the specific processing operation, contrary to the requirements of Article 6 GDPR.
Second, the DPA found a violation of the purpose limitation principle under Article 5(1)(b) GDPR. The controller had not demonstrated that forwarding the complaint to the employer was necessary to investigate the allegations. Instead, the employer provided information concerning the data subject's disciplinary history, which was unrelated to the matters he intended to report.
Third, the DPA held that the disclosure infringed the data minimisation principle under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. The controller could have requested further information from the data subject or contacted the employer without revealing his identity. The DPA emphasised that, even without an explicit confidentiality request, the controller should have taken precautions against the foreseeable risk of retaliation.
The DPA imposed a €5,000 fine, considering the significant impact on the data subject, the negligent nature of the infringement and the absence of previous violations.

title: BVwG - W274 2320278-1
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
An address publishing service and direct marketing company (the controller) sent the address data of a data subject to clients as part of its business activities. The clients are both end-customers who engage in sending communication e.g. for fund raising purposes, as well as industry partners that create and sell data sets to direct marketing companies. After the controller sends the personal data to its clients, it deletes the data.  
The controller is subject to the code of conduct for address publishing services and direct marketing companies pursuant to Article 40 GDPR. As far as the rights of the data subjects are concerned, according to the code of conduct, the controller is obliged to give full access to the data subjects’ data as provided for by Article 15 GDPR in case the controller is directly involved in the marketing communication. In case the controller provides the address data for a client’s marketing campaign and is therefore not involved in the direct marketing communication, the controller is obliged to instruct the client to provide in its communication with the data subjects the information that the address data has been obtained from the controller.  
The data subject is not on the so-called “Robinson list” for persons who do not wish to have their address data distributed for marketing purposes.  
The data subject requested access to their personal data from the controller, specifically concerning information about recipients and categories of recipients. The controller provided information on the categories of recipients but not the specific recipients. An additional access request by the data subject concerning information about the specific recipients was denied by the controller on the grounds that it is not possible to provide such information because of the sector specific practices in direct marketing. According to its deletion practice, the controller was not in possession of the requested data. 
Upon the subsequent complaint filed by the data subject with the DPA, the DPA held that the controller violated Article 15(1)(c) GDPR by not providing information on the specific recipients.  
The controller appealed the decision to the Austrian Federal Administrative Court (the court).  

Holding[edit | edit source]
The court held that the controller was not obliged under the GDPR to store the data about the specific recipients. However, the controller is obliged to comply with the principle of data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) as well as the principles of storage limitation (Article 5(1)(e) GDPR) and purpose limitation (Article 5(1)(b) GDPR). The storage period of personal data is to be reduced to the minimum. 
If there was a general obligation to store the data on the recipients, the controller would have to store that data for the sole purpose of answering to a theoretical access request by the data subject. This would contradict the logic of the data minimisation principle because the controller could always argue, when faced with a possible violation of the principles of data minimisation or storage limitation, that it stored the data for the purpose of a future access request.
According to the court, Article 11 GDPR and Recital 64 postulate the general principle that the data minimisation principle enjoys priority over an obligation to store data for the sole purpose of providing information in an access request.
In line with the jurisprudence of the CJEU, the court held that the court must balance the interest of the data subject to receive access to the information with the controller’s interest to delete the data in order not to be burdened with the storage of the data. Such a balancing of interest in the context of the storage period of data can also be derived from Article 24(1) GDPR that lays down the criteria to consider for the implementation of technical and organisational measures and the demonstration of compliance. Depending on the outcome of the balancing of interest, the controller can be obliged to protocol information on the recipients. This can be the case when the data concerned requires special protection.
In the specific case, the code of conduct for address publishers did not impose on the controller the obligation to store the data on the recipient. The code of conduct obliges the controller to give access to all data pursuant to Article 15 GDPR in case the controller has stored their own marketing data. Therefore, the storage of data is a prerequisite of the access request. But this provision does not deal with the obligation to store data.
The data subject’s right to data protection is not impaired because of the negation of a general obligation of the controller to store the data on recipients. This is because of the legal obligation under national law to provide direct marketing communication with an indication of the source from which the personal data has been obtained from. In case the direct marketing is conducted by a client of the controller, the controller is obliged to instruct the client to provide its communication with such an indication. Therefore, the source of their personal data is in any case communicated to the data subject.
According to the court, the data subject can also expect any third party that has obtained their data from the controller to actually contact the data subject and provide the information on where the data has been obtained from. This is because it would be economically disadvantageous for the client to buy the data and not use it for contacting the data subject, running the risk that the address of the data subject might become outdated.
The data subject did not make use of the possibility to be listed in the “Robinson list”, by which they would avoid the processing of their data by the controller.
On the other side, the interest of the controller not to be subject to an administrative burden by storing additional data, which runs counter the principle of data minimisation, must be considered.
Since the data in question does not enjoy special protection, the balancing of interest results in favour of the controller.

title: IMY (Sweden) - IMY-2025-21177
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
An IT company that provides digital HR and occupational health services (Miljödata) detected a data breach in August 2025. In the breach, an external attacker had gained unauthorised access to the personal data of approximately 2,200,000 individuals (the data subjects) by a ransomware attack, extracted this data from the systems, and published it on the dark web. Miljödata isolated all its servers and activated an external incident response team on the evening it detected the breach.
Miljödata reported the personal data breach to the DPA six days after it had happened. The attacker had gained access to the compromised data by performing a so-called SQL injection against a support component of a firewall solution that Miljödata had installed on a server in its technical environment. A limited number of children were among the data subjects affected. The data leaked included personal identification numbers, names, phone numbers, home addresses, email addresses, employment data, and sick leave information.
The DPA investigated whether Miljödata had implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk as required by Article 32(1) GDPR.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that Miljödata had violated Article 32(1) GDPR by failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures and issued the company a fine of SEK 1,800,000 (€160,000).
First, the DPA found that Miljödata had primarily acted as a processor and to a limited extent as a controller regarding the leaked data in its systems. As the obligation to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in Article 32(1) GDPR applies to both controllers and processors, the DPA did not assess Miljödata's role concerning each processing activity in detail.
Second, the DPA held that Miljödata had violated Article 32(1) GDPR. It considered the processing operations to pose high risks to the rights and freedoms of the data subjects. The processing was extensive – Miljödata had over 300 customers throughout Sweden, among them municipalities, regions, and other public entities. Moreover, the digital services Miljödata offered its customers involved extensive processing of sensitive personal data related to health, such as information on sick leave, data in rehabilitation documents, and information in medical certificates. The attacker had been present in Miljödata's technical environment for three days and gained access to additional information before the company's monitoring system had finally triggered an alert.
The DPA concluded that the technical and organisational measures implemented by Miljödata had not met the high level of security required for the processing at issue. The support component that enabled the breach contained a critical vulnerability, was new, and had not undergone testing before being integrated in Miljödata's firewall system.
When issuing the fine, the DPA held that Miljödata had acted negligently and  considered the violation of Article 32(1) GDPR to have been of a serious nature. It took into account that the processing had been extensive and that the GDPR violation concerned Miljödata’s core business, where the company could be presumed to be well-positioned to implement appropriate security measures.

title: ANSPDCP (Romania) - TIP TOP FOOD INDUSTRY SRL
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
TIP TOP FOOD INDUSTRY SRL (controller) used a time-and-attendance and access-control system on its employees at its premise. This system was using personal data in the form of the employees’ fingerprints. 
An individual lodged a complaint with the DPA.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the system used by the controller violated the principles of data minimisation (Article 5(1)(c) GDPR) and lawfulness because the controller could not rely on a legal basis for processing biometric data pursuant to Article 9 GDPR.  
According to the DPA, the controller could have used less intrusive means for the objectives of access control and time tracking and therefore violated Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.  
The DPA stressed that when processing biometric data, the controller must pay specific attention to the principles of lawfulness, necessity, data minimisation and proportionality. This is because of the significant risks arising from the processing of biometric data in case of unauthorized access and the possibility to link biometric data to the identity of the data subject. 
The DPA fined the controller RON 26,236 (€5,000). Additionally, the DPA ordered the controller to replace the access control and time-keeping system with an alternative system that is less intrusive and does not rely on the processing of biometric data, and thus complies with the principle of data minimisation.

title: UODO (Poland) - DKE.561.7.2026
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA launched an investigation into two websites operated by the controller under case number DKN.5101.8.2025. The controller collected the names and the occupations of individuals (the data subjects) and had not disclosed its identity and contact information on the websites.
The DPA requested the controller to provide information on the processing operations pursuant to Articles 58(1)(a) and 58(1)(e) GDPR. It attempted to contact the controller by sending it a letter on 15 April, an email on 15 May, and another email on 5 June. The DPA also called the business owner's contact number on 10 and 12 June, but the number was unavailable. 
Due to the unsuccessful attempts to contact the controller in connection with the proceedings in case DKN.5101.8.2025, the DPA initiated the administrative proceedings at issue against the controller. The controller was notified of this on June 15. The controller did not submit any additional explanations regarding the previous case, nor did it provide the data necessary to determine the basis for calculating the administrative fine in the present proceedings.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller had failed to provide the DPA access to personal data and other information it required for the performance of its tasks and issued the controller a fine of PLN 31,507 (€7,200). It found that the controller had violated Articles 58(1)(a) and 58(1)(e) GDPR.

title: Persónuvernd (Island) - 2025061555
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA initiated an investigation into Isavia domestic airports Ltd. (the controller) concerning the electronic monitoring of car parks in five airports: Reykjavík, Akureyri, Egilsstaðir, Ísafjörður and Sauðárkrókur.
The investigation followed a complaint received on 16 September 2024 concerning the use of automatic number plate recognition cameras for parking fee collection at Reykjavík and Akureyri airports, allegedly without adequate signage informing individuals of the monitoring.
On 20 March 2025, the DPA opened a preliminary examination of the controller's processing of personal data. Following an assessment of the controller's response, the DPA initiated formal proceedings on 30 June 2025 to determine whether the electronic monitoring complied with the transparency and information requirements under the GDPR and national data protection legislation.
The controller used CCTV and number plate recognition cameras for parking fee collection, security and asset protection. It maintained that signs were present in the monitored areas and that further information, including the purposes and legal basis of the processing, was available through its privacy policy, which could be accessed using QR codes displayed on the signs.
However, the controller acknowledged that, at Akureyri Airport, vehicles could be recorded by number plate recognition cameras before drivers encountered the relevant signs. At Ísafjörður and Sauðárkrókur airports, the existing signs were located within the monitored areas and did not identify the controller or indicate where further information about the processing could be obtained.
During the proceedings, the controller updated its privacy policy and installed or replaced signs at several airports. In particular, it installed additional signs at Akureyri Airport and repositioned the signs at Ísafjörður Airport to inform individuals before they entered the monitored areas. The controller also discontinued electronic monitoring at Sauðárkrókur Airport and removed the surveillance cameras.
On 22 December 2025, the controller informed the DPA that it had completed the improvements.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found that the controller had violated the transparency principle under Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and its information obligations under Articles 12 and 13 GDPR, as well as the corresponding requirements under national data protection legislation.
The DPA considered that the signage and information provided at both Reykjavík and Egilsstaðir airports had, in principle, complied with Article 13 GDPR. In the Akureyi, Ísafjörður and Sauðárkrókur airports, the DPA considered that the warning of license plate and general camera surveillance was not provided prior to entering the monitored area. The DPA further held that at Ísafjörður and Sauðárkrókur airports, the information provided was also materially inadequate as the signs did not identify the controller or indicate where further information could be obtained. At all three airports, the signs were not positioned to inform individuals before entering the monitored areas.
The DPA recalled that Articles 12 and 13 GDPR require controllers to provide accessible information at the time personal data are collected. It also emphasised that individuals must be informed of video surveillance before entering monitored areas.
Since the controller had subsequently improved its signage and privacy policy and discontinued monitoring at Sauðárkrókur Airport, the DPA considered that no further corrective measures were necessary.
Taking into account the limited scope of the monitoring, the improvements implemented and the principle of proportionality under Article 83(1) GDPR, the DPA issued a reprimand without imposing an administrative fine.

title: Persónuvernd (Iceland) - 2025020567
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received a request from a the NPA Centre, the service manager of services for disabled people with long-term care needs, asking whether the Social Services Department of the City of Reykjavik (the controller) is permitted to request personal data. This included bank statements and receipts from the members of the centre relating to expenses for the services of support workers who provide user-directed personal assistance (NPA).
In the request, it was made evident that the NPA Centre receives funds from the local authority and distributes it accordingly to its members and supporting staff. Disabled individuals are the line managers and the centre is the employer of the individual’s support workers receiving their timesheets and correspondingly paid their wages.
It was further established that the personal data requested by the controller would provide the local authority with comprehensive insight into the life, lifestyle, interests, events, social participation and daily activities of disabled individuals that are with NPA. Thus, the NPA held that the request for the collection of this data goes beyond the legal authority of the controller, is unreasonable and unnecessary.
The controller claimed no personal data processing was being undertaken. However, deemed the collection of such necessary to obtain detailed monitoring of the use of funds as some individuals had accumulated high sums of money.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that in line with complying with its legal obligations, the controller may be able to process personal data including sensitive data in connection to monitoring the expenditure of funds allocated for NPA. Nonetheless, the DPA found that the current planned collection of personal data by the controller from the NPA Centre is not compatible with the GDPR and the national data protection act.
The DPA clarified that processing must comply with the principles enshrined in Article 5 GDPR particularly transparency and proportionality. The DPA emphasised that collecting such data from all NPA users spendings, irrespective of individual instances, without exhausting less intrusive alternatives would be incompatible with the principle of proportionality and unnecessary. This was considered in connection with the fact that the collection of this personal data indicates a significant amount of information including sensitive data about the daily life and activities undertaken by individuals concerned.
The DPA further clarified that in compliance with the principle of transparency, the Social Services Department must ensure that the users of NPA are sufficiently informed that they may be required to provide this data in certain circumstances.

title: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italy) - 10297167
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The DPA received two distinct but related complaints from employees (the data subjects) of the National Institute of Meteorological Research (the controller) concerning the transparency of the use of video surveillance.
The controller clarified that the surveillance was subject to a trade agreement within which they were testing the use and coverage of 10 cameras. The cameras would only record when the alarm was activated, and excluded the possibility of recording areas which were subject to public access. Storage of the recordings was limited to 72 hours from the trigger of an alarm.
The controller further explained that at the time the surveillance system was being tested without actually recording any images. Particularly, the controller sought to verify the technical and adequate functioning of the cameras and monitors as well as effective coverage of the security parameter.
Due to insufficient and inadequate coverage of certain areas, which was deemed contrary to the purpose of the surveillance, the controller subsequently installed 8 additional cameras. The controller clarified that this was in line with the agreement which allowed for extraordinary maintenance.
As a result of the surveillance being at the testing phase, the controller did not provide the data subjects and staff of the information regarding data processing. The controller emphasised that before its official operation this information would be provided.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the installed cameras were incompatible with the agreement as a result of increasing the number of cameras as well as the modification of their location and subsequent area being converted. Nonetheless, the DPA found that the extraordinary maintenance did not allow for the defined area being covered by the cameras to be altered. Therefore, although the purpose of surveillance activation was to test the system, personal data processing was still being undertaken.
The DPA further emphasised that the controller failed to inform its staff and interested parties sufficiently of the surveillance practices, neither of the associated personal data processing happening, prior to its implementation. The DPA held that the lack of information and the fact that the signage was affixed after the processing had already taken place was insufficient.
Finally, the DPA found that the controller implemented the video surveillance in its workplace, which considered of the processing of personal data of its employees, in absence of the necessary data protection impact assessment, contrary to Article 35 GDPR.
In light of the foregoing the DPA fined the controller €10,000 for violations of Articles 5(1)(a), 12, 13, 35 and 88 GDPR.

title: BVwG - W254 2314468-1
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject sent an access request to the service provider (the processor). It replied that it held no personal data concerning the data subject in its capacity as controller. It explained that it provided services to N-GmbH and acted as its processor.
The processor and N-GmbH belonged to the same corporate group. The data subject had received payment demands from a debt collection agency in 2020 and 2021 that identified the processor as the instructing party and also received demands from a law firm in 2020 and 2024 referring to the processor as its client.
The DPA initially rejected the data subject's complaint in 2023. In 2025, the Federal Administrative Court partially voided the decision because the DPA had not adequately investigated whether the processor had processed the data in connection with the debt collection and litigation activities, including whether those activities fell within the processing agreement with N-GmbH. The court upheld the rejection of the data subject's other requests.
Following the remittal, the DPA again rejected the data protection complaint. The data subject appealed, arguing that the controller had acted in its own name and therefore as controller rather than processor.


Holding[edit | edit source]
First, the court distinguished between a controller and a processor by focusing on who actually decided the purposes and essential means of the processing. A processor could not freely determine those elements because it processed personal data on behalf of the controller.
Second, the court found that the processor had been commissioned by N-GmbH to handle payment processing, including payment reminders and the handling of legal cases. The payment demands and reminder sent to the data subject therefore formed part of the tasks assigned to the processor and were covered by the processing agreement. The court found no evidence that it had exceeded the authority given to it under that agreement.
The court therefore concluded that N-GmbH, as controller, was responsible for responding to the data subject's access request and the processor did not have a separate obligation to provide the requested information beyond its processor role. 
The court upheld the DPA's decision and dismissed the data subject's complaint as unfounded.

title: AEPD (Spain) - ps-00287-2025
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA against the Dirección General de Tráfico (DGT), the controller, the Spanish public authority responsible for traffic management, road safety and the administration of driving licences and vehicle records, after discovering that its mobile app transmitted numerous categories of personal and device data to a third-party service provider, the processor.
The controller explained that the processor's software was integrated into the app to provide push notifications. However, the integration also enabled an optional functionality which transmitted usage and device data that were not necessary for providing those notifications.
During its investigation, the DPA found that different versions of the app transmitted data including IP addresses, device information, country, language, app identifiers and information concerning the user's mobile network operator.
The controller acknowledged that older versions of the app had transmitted personal data unnecessarily and implemented technical changes aimed at stopping the collection and transmission of such data.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the controller violated Article 5(1)(c) GDPR because the app collected and transmitted personal data that were not necessary for its intended purposes.
In particular, the DPA considered that information such as IP addresses, country and mobile network operator data exceeded what was necessary for the app's functionality. The DPA also considered IP addresses to be personal data because they can allow a user to be identified when combined with other information.
The controller's subsequent technical changes did not remove the infringement that had already occurred. Therefore, the DPA found a violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.
Since the controller was a public authority subject to Article 77 LOPDGDD, the DPA declared the infringement without imposing an administrative fine.

title: Ss. v Nitra - 53Cpr/1/2023
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
A kindergarten teacher, the data subject, has been working for the Municipality of Malý Lapáš, the controller, since January 2016. On 4 July 2023, the controller immediately terminated the data subject's employment on the basis of a serious breach of work discipline. The controller relied on two incidents. First, the data subject had allegedly left the workplace shortly before the end of her working hours without the consent of her superior. Second, she had published photographs of children from the kindergarten on her private Facebook profile.
The photographs were taken during an overnight kindergarten event. The data subject published seven photographs alongside a post thanking a local pizzeria for providing sponsored pizza to the children. She maintained that she had tried to avoid showing the children's faces and that her intention was merely to thank the sponsor.
The controller argued that the photographs constituted personal data and that the data subject was not authorised to publish them on her private Facebook account. Parents provided an informed consent at the beginning of each school year which permitted the publication of photographs through specified channels, including the municipality's website, the kindergarten's official website, EduPage and within the kindergarten premises. This consent did not cover publication on an employee's private Facebook profile.
The data subject admitted that she did not have prior written consent from the children's legal representatives for publication on her private account. She considered the general informed consent sufficient and claimed that the parents had been aware of the planned publication. After the termination of her employment, she attempted to obtain additional consent from the parents.
The data subject challenged the immediate termination before the Court and requested a declaration that the termination was invalid as well as compensation for lost wages.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The Court upheld the data subject's claim and declared the immediate termination of her employment invalid.
Regarding the photographs, the Court held that the overnight kindergarten event was connected to the data subject's employment. She therefore remained bound by her confidentiality obligations under § 79 Act No. 18/2018 on Personal Data Protection.
The Court considered that, under Article 5 GDPR, the publication of the children's photographs on the data subject's private Facebook profile required prior consent from their legal representatives. The general informed consent signed by the parents did not cover publication on a private social-media account, as it was limited to specified channels used by the kindergarten.
Since the data subject had published the photographs without prior parental consent, despite having received data-protection training and being bound by confidentiality obligations, the Court found that she had breached her data-protection and employment duties, including § 81(f) Labour Code.
However, the Court held that the breach was not serious enough to justify immediate termination under § 68(1)(b) Labour Code. It considered the circumstances of the publication, the data subject's intention to thank a sponsor, her attempt to limit the children's identifiability, her previous work record, the absence of proven complaints and the lack of demonstrated damage to the controller.
The Court also found that the controller had not sufficiently proven that the data subject's early departure from the workplace constituted a serious breach of work discipline.
Consequently, the Court held that immediate termination was disproportionate and declared it invalid. The claim for compensation for lost wages was separated into independent proceedings. No GDPR fine or other data-protection corrective measure was imposed.

title: AEPD (Spain) - PS/00339/2024
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The father of the data subject, who is a minor, submitted a complaint after registering his daughter with the Royal Spanish Soccer Federation (RFEF). In order to apply, the controller requested the father to provide, amongst other documentation, a certificate of municipal registration and a school certificate (as supporting documentation), to verify the required uninterrupted five-year residence in Spain.
According to the FIFA guidelines for submitting applications for minors, for first time applications the player must have lived continuously for five years in the country where they are being registered. FIFA’s guidelines require a residence certificate and as an alternative the school certificate of the minor.
The controller explained that this procedure and the requested documents is a result of a long-established procedure by FIFA, which required both the residence certificate and the minors school certificate.


Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA found the requirement by FIFA of proof of residence for a player whose registration is sought through a certificate of residence, a logical and reasonable exception to the prohibition of international transfers of minors. Nonetheless, according to the controller the school transcripts were required as supporting documentation, which implied that they are required in addition to the certificate of municipal registration.
The DPA held that requesting and requiring both documents violated the principle of data minimisation, and deemed the requesting of one of the two documents sufficient to prove uninterrupted residence. This was considered in addition to the fact that FIFA’s guidelines explicitly state the alternative nature of the documents.
Therefore, DPA held that the controller required, for player registration, documentation from the play which contained personal data exceeding what is officially required by FIFA.  The DPA emphasised the importance of data protection for minors and how such a requirement involves more processing than necessary which could potentially expose minors to unnecessary risks.
In light of the foregoing, the DPA fined the controller €100,000 for the violation of the data minimisation principle, enshrined in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

title: High Court - 2026 IEHC 640
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties (ICCL), a qualified entity, brought a representative action against Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited concerning the processing of personal data through the Xandr real-time bidding platform. ICCL alleged that personal data broadcast during real-time bidding auctions could include highly personal information and that the processing infringed several GDPR requirements, including transparency, data minimisation, security and consent obligations. It sought injunctive relief requiring Microsoft to cease, amend or restrict the processing.
A dispute subsequently arose concerning the burden of proof and the parties' pleading obligations. ICCL argued that Articles 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR required the controller to demonstrate its compliance with the GDPR. Microsoft disputed that it was the relevant controller and argued that the ordinary rules of civil procedure placed the burden of establishing the alleged infringements on ICCL.
The parties also disagreed about the information that had to be provided in the representative action. Microsoft sought further information concerning, among other things, the alleged infringements, the consumers affected and the funding of the proceedings. The High Court therefore determined several preliminary questions relating to the burden of proof, pleading requirements and access to information before the underlying GDPR allegations were decided.

Holding[edit | edit source]
The High Court held that Articles 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR do not create a general reversal of the legal or evidential burden of proof. The claimant must first establish the matters for which it bears the burden, including that the defendant is a controller and that processing takes place which engages the relevant GDPR obligations.
However, once those matters are established and compliance with a relevant GDPR obligation is at issue, the controller bears the legal and evidential burden of demonstrating compliance. In particular, where compliance with the principles in Article 5(1) GDPR or with the requirements covered by Article 24(1) GDPR must be determined, it is for the controller to prove that the relevant processing complies with those obligations. The Court considered this to follow from the accountability obligations.
The High Court further held that the ordinary national rules on pleadings continue to apply to both parties. Each party must plead the material facts supporting the matters it is required to prove. Consequently, where the controller wishes to advance a positive case that it complied with the GDPR, it must plead the material facts on which that claim of compliance is based.
Regarding the representative action, the High Court held that Sections 19(10) and 19(11) of the Representative Actions for the Protection of the Collective Interests of Consumers Act 2023 do not give the controller a standalone right to require the claimant to provide further information. However, the controller may rely on ordinary procedural mechanisms, including requests for particulars, discovery or disclosure under Section 34(2), where the applicable requirements are met, and may challenge the admissibility of the representative action.
The High Court did not determine whether the processing through the Xandr platform actually infringed the GDPR. It also declined to determine certain additional questions, including the application of the "peculiar knowledge principle", because the necessary facts had not been agreed. No fine or corrective measure was imposed.

title: DSB (Austria) - 2025-0.626.844
text:
English Summary[edit | edit source]
Facts[edit | edit source]
The data subject requested access to their personal data from a video streaming service (controller) established in the US. The controller provided access to certain personal data in “opml” and “json” format. The controller’s reply did not include information on personal data from tracking, cookies, web profile, purposes of processing, recipients, storage periods, data subjects’ rights, right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority, sources of personal data and data transfers to third countries. 
For further information, the controller referred the data subject to general information on their privacy statement and to different online tools provided by the controller on a portal. There was no single tool where the data subject could download all requested data. The controller indicated that the data subject shall contact customer service in case they cannot access all the requested personal data on the tools. 
The data subject lodged a complaint with the DPA, claiming a violation of their access right. 



Holding[edit | edit source]
The DPA held that the GDPR was applicable pursuant to Article 3(2)(a) GDPR because the controller, despite being established outside the EU, offered their services within the EU. 
By providing the personal data in “opml” and “json” format, the controller violated the principle of transparency provided for in Article 12(1) GDPR. This is because these formats are used for machine processing and are not easily accessible and intelligible for the data subject. The right to access does not only encompass the mere access to the data, but also the preparation thereof in an intelligible and accessible format that data subjects who are not specialised in IT can understand. 
In order for the controller to comply with Article 12 GDPR and Article 15 GDPR, the controller must give full access to the data. A portal where the data subject must rely on several tools in order to receive access to their personal data, and to request from customer service any information that is not provided via the tools, does not fulfil this criterium. The data subject cannot be expected to identify any missing information since the data subject does not know what personal data the controller processes. It is the purpose of the access right to provide the data subject with the knowledge about the data that the controller processes about them.
The controller did not comply with Article 15 GDPR by referring the data subject to the privacy statement. The privacy statement includes ex ante information in order to fulfil the obligations of Article 13 GDPR and Article 14 GDPR. The general information on the processing of the controller is not necessarily applicable to the individual case of the data subject. The controller cannot fulfil its obligation to give access by providing general information.
As far as the purposes of processing are concerned, the DPA held that the controller must provide information on the specific purposes of processing for the specific case of the data subject in order to comply with Article 15(1)(a) GDPR. The data subject must be able to identify which categories of personal data about them are processed for what purpose. The same is true for the storage period. Therefore, the DPA found a violation of Article 15(1)(a) GDPR and Article 15(1)(d) GDPR. 
As far as the sources of data, the recipients, and appropriate safeguards for data transfers to third countries are concerned, the DPA held that the referral to the general information in the privacy statement did not suffice either. The privacy statement merely included general remarks such as the possible categories of data, the fact that the data can be collected from specific sources and that a certain legal framework in the light of data transfers to third countries is followed. Therefore, the controller violated Article 15(1) GDPR and Article 15(2) GDPR
Because of the economic size of the controller, a globally acting cooperation, the provision of the requested information can be expected from the controller.
